newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS - FEB 6.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS - FEB 6.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--Violations and infringements of Greek air space by Turkish fighter planes increased a worrying 636 percent in 1996 over 1995 figures. The figures indicate a qualitative as well as quantitative upgrading of Turkish provocations in the Aegean.

--The finance and health ministries will place an upper limit on the number of times Greece's civil servants can visit their doctors, in an effort to contain ever-increasing health spending in the public sector. Civil servants visit their doctors three times more often that workers insured under the national health system and five times more often than those with limited health cover.

--Ten ministers are being dispatched to the countryside to use thier persuasive powers on defiant farmers, following Prime Minister Costas Simitis's dramatic call at yesterday's inner cabinet meeting to support the government's policies or else put the future of the government and country at stake.

--Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas lashes out at the "old" ruling party PASOK, the Communist Party and the media over the latest farmers' crisis, adding that national roads will remain open "at all cost".
--Farmers in Thessaly meanwhile have called for a meeting with Simitis, following their agreement to continue their protests.

--And on the schools front, striking high school teachers decided to continue for a fourth week. They marched rowdily through downtown Athens yesterday (following an earlier march by construction workers), causing havoc to traffic and having two of their number arrested.
--Despite a court order to close down, the Greek Centre of Applied Philosophy (KEFE) has simply changed its name - to Greek Centre for Dianetics and Scientology - and continues to operate.

--Reports state that half of ruling party PASOK is kicking back in reaction to the government's policies: criticism over its handling of the strikes and farmers' protests came from Education Minister Gerasimos Arsenis and a clutch of other leading cadres.

--Conservative opposition New Democracy leader Miltiades Evert applauded the decision of 31 ND deputies to reiterate their determination that there be no compromise on the issue of a name for the Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia.

--For students, the 1996-97 school year is in doubt: the strike has cost students 100 hours of lessons. When teachers return to their classrooms, students are likely to face increased school hours and loss of holidays to make up for lost time.
